title: Vishvamitra becomes a seer
hookLine: a king loses to a sage, chases the sage's title for years, and finds the real fight is inside him
carry: tapas: he had to win against himself
tomorrow: a warrior drops his bow. what does Krishna say can never be lost?

lines: A KING LOSES TO A SAGE.
cards: The king has just lost, and he can't believe it. He rode into a forest hermitage with an army, wanting one thing the sage Vasishtha had: a cow that could give whatever was asked of her. Vasishtha wouldn't part with her.
The army couldn't take her. So King Vishvamitra sets down his bow and makes a new plan. If a seer beat him, he'll become a seer.
He leaves the throne for long, hard austerity, and in the Ramayana's telling, the god Brahma finally comes to him with a title. The king hears it, and he's furious.

teach.h: RAJARSHI: A ROYAL SEER, A CEILING.
teach.b: The title Brahma gives him is rajarshi: raja, king, and rishi, seer, joined into one word. A royal seer. To most ears, an honor.
To Vishvamitra, a ceiling: still a king first. He wanted brahmarshi, the title Vasishtha held. So he goes back to tapas.

The word means heat: the inner fire of discipline, fasting, stillness, keeping a vow. Hindus have honored it since the Vedas as the way a person is changed from inside. And here's what makes his story worth telling.
The hardships aren't what nearly beat him. He is. The apsara Menaka is sent to him, and he forgets his vow for ten years.
Later he loses his temper and curses the apsara Rambha, and the fire he'd built drains away again.

The Gita names those two as the enemy inside a person. So Vishvamitra takes the hardest vow of all: no more anger, and silence. Only then does Brahma call him brahmarshi, and Vasishtha, the old rival, greets him by it.

teach.h: THE TITLE CAME WHEN HE STOPPED FIGHTING FOR IT.
teach.b: Many teachers read the ending this way: the title came when he no longer needed to beat anyone for it. And tradition remembers him for something bigger.
It names him the seer of the Gayatri, the verse many Hindus recite at dawn, asking the divine light to stir our minds. A prayer for a clear mind, from a man who had to burn through his own.

how: Many Hindus make a sankalpa, a short spoken vow, before a fast or a puja; the Gayatri, credited by tradition to Vishvamitra, is recited at dawn by those who keep it.

o: a chant repeated at dawn by a seer
how sounds change where two words meet
a title for a king who leaves his throne

games.q: the king's long climb — tap the pairs.
p: raja + rishi: a royal seer, and a ceiling
heat: the inner fire of discipline
desire, then anger, drained his fire
the title he won once he'd mastered himself

s: Vishvamitra won his title by finally beating Vasishtha
armies and curses failed. he was called brahmarshi after he conquered his own anger, and Vasishtha greeted him by it.
tapas means heat: the inner fire of discipline that changes a person
fasting, stillness, keeping a vow: honored since the Vedas.
the fasting was too hard, so his tapas kept failing
the hardships weren't what broke it. desire, then anger, did.

games.q: at a family puja, an uncle says Vishvamitra became a great seer because he was born a king. what does the story say?
o: he left the throne, and became one through tapas, once he'd mastered his own anger.
his birth made it easy: the title came with the crown.
Vasishtha handed it over to end their fight.
games.why: the throne was the thing he left behind. the title came after long tapas, and only after he stopped letting desire and anger burn it away.

practice: Bring to mind one moment this week when wanting or anger took the wheel. Don't scold yourself. Then make a small vow, the way Hindus do before a fast or a puja: a sankalpa, one plain sentence, for one day.
If you pray, offer it; if not, simply say it to yourself. Then sit still with the breath, the way Vishvamitra finally sat.

wordCard.voice: Sandhi plainly: where words meet and lean together. Raja and rishi become rajarshi; maha and rishi, maharshi. Even a seer's title is two plain words, joined.

orig.note: Sanskrit: a royal seer, from raja, king, and rishi, seer; a and ri join as ar.

carryVoice: Keep this one: tapas, he had to win against himself. His real rival was never Vasishtha. Day done.

sources.ref: Valmiki Ramayana, Bala Kanda (Vishvamitra and Vasishtha: the cow, the tapas, Menaka and Rambha, the titles rajarshi, maharshi and brahmarshi)
Ashtadhyayi 6.1.87 (ad gunah) with 1.1.51 (ri strengthened as ar)
Rig Veda 3.62.10 (the Gayatri), credited by tradition to Vishvamitra
Bhagavad Gita 3.37 (desire and anger named as the enemy within)
